hints: Think about what volatility really means, how easily a liquid turns to vapour and escapes from intermolecular forces.
Compare $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Br}_2$, bromine has many more electrons so its electron cloud is larger and more easily distorted.
Link stronger instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces to harder evaporation, then pick the element with weaker forces as more volatile.
walkthrough:
**Recall what volatility means**

Think of volatility as how keen a substance is to evaporate. A more volatile liquid has weaker intermolecular forces holding its particles together, so it escapes easily.

Rule to remember:
$$\text{weaker intermolecular forces} \rightarrow \text{more volatile (lower boiling point)}$$

**Identify the forces in chlorine and bromine**

Both $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{Br}_2$ are simple non-polar molecules. The only forces between their molecules are instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces.

**Compare the strength of the forces**

Bromine has more electrons (35 per atom) than chlorine (17 per atom) and a larger electron cloud. This makes $\text{Br}_2$ more polarisable, so temporary dipoles form more easily and the forces are stronger.

Comparison:
$$\text{strength of London forces: Br}_2 > \text{Cl}_2$$

**Deduce the more volatile element**

Because $\text{Cl}_2$ has weaker forces, less energy is needed to separate its molecules, so it evaporates more readily. That is why chlorine is a gas at room temperature while bromine is a liquid. This matches the row with chlorine as more volatile and stronger forces in bromine.

options.A: Incorrect identity. The explanation part is correct that forces are greater in bromine, but stronger forces mean less volatile, not more. Bromine is a liquid at room temperature while chlorine is a gas, so bromine cannot be more volatile.
options.B: Both parts are wrong. Bromine is not more volatile than chlorine, and forces are not greater in chlorine. This reverses the trend: larger molecules with more electrons have stronger, not weaker, London forces.
options.C: Correct on both counts. Chlorine is more volatile because its instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces are weaker. Bromine has more electrons and is more polarisable, so its forces are stronger and it is held as a liquid more strongly.
options.D: Correct identity but wrong explanation. Chlorine is indeed more volatile, but its forces are weaker, not stronger, than those in bromine. Stronger forces would lower volatility, so this explanation contradicts the identity.
